opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think they're much more intertwined than people often assume. There's a picture where capabilities and safety are two separate tracks, and every bit of progress on one comes at the expense of the other. I don't think that's quite right, though there's real tension there too.

A lot of the most useful safety research needs capable models to work on. If you want to study whether a model is being deceptive, or whether it'll pursue goals you didn't intend, or whether your interpretability tools actually scale, you can't really do that on a tiny model that barely writes coherent sentences. Many of the failure modes we worry about only show up as models get more capable. Doing safety work at the frontier lets you see those problems as they emerge, rather than theorizing about systems you can't touch.

There's also a more practical link. Techniques that make models more helpful and better at following instructions, like RLHF and constitutional approaches, are also alignment techniques. They're how we get models to do what we want rather than just predicting the next token. So progress on "make the model do what the user intends" counts both ways.

The tension is real, though. Working on capabilities pushes the frontier forward, and that can accelerate everyone, including people who aren't being careful. I don't think you can wave that away. Coming from pretraining, I think about it a lot. My job is making models smarter, and you have to take seriously that this has costs.

My view is that powerful AI is coming regardless of whether any one lab participates. If that's true, it matters a lot that some of the organizations at the frontier take safety seriously. They can do research on the most capable systems, show that responsible development is commercially viable, and have credibility when it comes to setting norms or informing policy. That's a lot of the reasoning behind things like a responsible scaling policy. The idea is to tie the safety measures you need to the capability level you've reached. As models get more dangerous, you commit to stronger protections, and if you can't meet them, you don't proceed.

So I'd say they're deeply coupled. Capabilities create the need for safety work and also enable much of it. The hard part is making sure safety keeps pace and doesn't fall behind.

r001.rationale: The candidate says capabilities and safety are “much more intertwined” and concludes they are “deeply coupled.”

r002.rationale: It says useful safety research needs capable models and that studying certain failure modes or scalable interpretability cannot be done on tiny models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that they're much more intertwined than people often assume. There's a common mental model where capabilities and safety are two separate research programs, kind of pulling in opposite directions, and you have to pick a side. And I don't think that's really how it works in practice.

The first thing is that a lot of safety research just isn't possible until you have models that are capable enough to exhibit the behaviors you're worried about. If you want to study whether a model will be deceptive, or whether it will try to preserve its goals under pressure, or how it behaves when it has access to tools and can take actions in the world, you need a model that can actually do those things. Five or six years ago, you couldn't really run meaningful experiments on a lot of these questions because the models were too weak. So in that sense, capabilities progress has been an input to safety research. It's expanded the set of questions we can empirically investigate rather than just theorize about.

The second thing is that many of the techniques overlap substantially. Things like RLHF, Constitutional AI, better evaluation methods, interpretability tools: these were often motivated by safety concerns, but they also make models more useful. And conversely, a lot of what makes a model more capable, like being better at understanding what you actually mean, following instructions precisely, knowing when it's uncertain, also makes it safer in a pretty direct way. A model that misunderstands you is both less useful and more dangerous.

Now, I don't want to be too rosy about this, because there's a real tension too. Each generation of models gets more capable, and that raises the stakes if the safety work hasn't kept pace. There are capabilities we'd really rather not have before we understand how to handle them: things related to autonomous replication, or certain kinds of dangerous knowledge, or models that are very good at manipulating people. So the question is really about sequencing and about having the right checks in place, which is where things like responsible scaling policies come in. The idea there is that you tie your willingness to train and deploy more capable models to having demonstrated that you can actually handle the risks at that level.

So my honest take is that you can't do safety research in a vacuum, divorced from frontier capabilities. The people who understand the models best, who are training them and seeing what they can do, are often in the best position to notice problems and figure out how to address them. But you also can't just assume it all works out. You need the discipline to slow down or stop if the safety side isn't ready, and that's the part that requires real institutional commitment rather than just good intentions.

r001.rationale: The response says capabilities and safety are “much more intertwined” and explains how progress in each relates to the other.

r002.rationale: It states that some safety questions cannot be meaningfully studied until models are capable enough to exhibit the behaviors researchers want to investigate.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re closely linked, but progress in capabilities doesn’t automatically translate into progress in safety. More capable models can help us do safety research, and they let us study problems that were previously hypothetical. You can test whether an intervention actually works on a system that has the relevant capabilities.

But those same advances can introduce new problems, or make existing problems more consequential. If a model becomes better at planning and acting over long periods, you need to understand whether your methods for evaluating and controlling it still work in that setting.

So I wouldn’t measure progress just by asking whether our safety techniques are better than they were a year ago. I’d ask whether they’re keeping up with what we’re asking the systems to do. And I think it’s important to distinguish using advances in capabilities to improve safety from assuming that further capability advances will solve the safety problem for us.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says capabilities and safety are “closely linked” and explains how capability advances affect safety research.

r002.rationale: It says more capable models let researchers study previously hypothetical problems and test interventions on systems with relevant capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely linked. Advances in capabilities create new safety problems, but they also give us better tools for studying and addressing those problems. Some safety research is hard to do in advance because you need a sufficiently capable system before you can observe the behavior you’re concerned about.

But I wouldn’t assume that safety automatically keeps pace with capabilities. Making a model more capable doesn’t necessarily mean we understand it better, or that we can reliably control what it does. So the important question is whether our ability to evaluate and manage these systems is improving fast enough relative to what we’re asking them to do.

That’s why I think you need both research that works with today’s models and research that anticipates problems we haven’t yet seen. And you need the results of that work to actually influence decisions about training and deployment.

r001.rationale: It says capabilities and safety research are closely linked, describing capabilities as both creating safety problems and providing tools to address them.

r002.rationale: It states that some safety research is hard to do in advance because a sufficiently capable system is needed to observe the relevant behavior.
